predecessors.name: County of Savoy
predecessors.text: Savoy and Piedmont as the House of Savoy held them: the same state as the County and Duchy of Savoy, which Cliopatria splits into two rows at 1539/1564

predecessors.name: Kingdom of France
predecessors.text: the lands France held in occupation 1536-59 and gave back at the Peace of Cateau-Cambresis

successors.name: Kingdom of Sardinia
successors.text: the Savoyard lands of 1720 with the island of Sardinia; Sicily had passed to Austria

rulers.name: Victor Amadeus II
rulers.title: Duke of Savoy, King of Sicily from 1713, King of Sardinia from 1720

ledger.x: 1559: the Peace of Cateau-Cambresis restores Emmanuel Philibert to the duchy after the French occupation of 1536-59.
1562: Emmanuel Philibert moves the capital from Chambery to Turin.
1564: Savoy recovers the lands round Geneva from Bern.
1588: Charles Emmanuel I occupies the Marquisate of Saluzzo.
1601: the occupation of Saluzzo ends in a treaty.
1601: the Treaty of Lyon gives Saluzzo to Savoy.
1601: the Treaty of Lyon takes Bresse, Bugey and Gex from Savoy.
March 1629: France takes Pinerolo.
1630: France overruns Savoy.
6 April 1631: the Treaty of Cherasco ends the war: 'All foreign troops are to be withdrawn' (a second agreement of 19 June 1631 confirmed it and 'added rules for withdrawing troops').
6 April 1631: Pinerolo, held by France since March 1629, is 'awarded to France' by the Treaty of Cherasco, which turns the occupation into a cession (the loss entry that follows).
1631: the Treaty of Cherasco gives Savoy the Montferrat towns of Trino and Alba.
1631: Pinerolo goes to France under the Treaty of Cherasco.
1690: France occupies Savoyard lands in the Nine Years' War.
1696: the Treaty of Turin returns the occupied lands.
1696: Pinerolo returns to Savoy after its fortifications are destroyed.
1703: France occupies Savoy again.
1703: France holds western Piedmont.
September 1706: the relief of Turin frees the Piedmontese lands.
1707: France occupies the County of Nice.
1708: Montferrat passes to Savoy.
1713: France gives Savoy back.
1713: France gives the County of Nice back.
1713: Victor Amadeus II receives the Kingdom of Sicily.
11 April 1713: parts of the Duchy of Milan pass to Savoy.
1713: Savoy gives the Ubaye Valley (Barcelonnette) to France.
1713: Savoy receives the Italian Dauphine in exchange.
1718: Spain invades Sicily.
1719: Austrian forces retake Sicily from Spain.
1719: Austria holds Sicily after retaking it.
1720: Austrian occupation of Sicily ends in the cession.
1720: Savoy cedes Sicily to Austria.
1720: Austria cedes Sardinia to Savoy.
1720: the Duchy of Savoy becomes the Kingdom of Sardinia.

wars.name: First Monferrato war
wars.outcome: Ended with a compromise signed in Paris and Madrid in September 1617; the page records no change of frontier.

wars.name: War of the Mantuan Succession
wars.outcome: Treaty of Cherasco, 6 April 1631 (confirmed 19 June): Trino and Alba to Savoy, Savoy renounces other claims to Montferrat, Pinerolo awarded to France.

wars.name: Nine Years' War (Savoyard front)
wars.outcome: Savoy made a separate peace with France in the Treaty of Turin (29 August 1696): all occupied territories returned, including Pinerolo; the Convention of Vigevano (7 October 1696) set a general ceasefire in Italy.

wars.name: War of the Spanish Succession (Savoyard front)
wars.outcome: Turin relieved in September 1706; Montferrat passed to Savoy in 1708; at Utrecht in 1713 Savoy received Sicily and parts of the Duchy of Milan (11 April 1713) and the Dauphine valleys beyond the Alps, gave the Ubaye Valley to France, and France gave back…

wars.name: War of the Quadruple Alliance
wars.outcome: Treaty of The Hague, 17 February 1720: Savoy cedes Sicily to Austria and receives Sardinia.

certainty.note: The restored duchy's extent is bridged from Cliopatria; no page opened gives the Alpine or Lake Geneva frontiers or the places held by foreign garrisons.
Frontiers fixed by dated treaties: Lyon (17 January 1601), Cherasco (6 April 1631), Turin (29 August 1696), Utrecht (11 April 1713) and The Hague (17 February 1720).
